human_tolerance.notes: Seemingly unfazed by considerable human activity: it can nest and live in close proximity to large numbers of humans, is found in cities where rock pigeons and brown rats support the population, and took readily to the utility poles and treeless medians of new highways. Historic settlement helped it, since clearing forest in the Northeast made hunting areas while woodlots left nest sites.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Reaches sexual maturity at two years and is monogamous, mating with the same individual for many years and usually taking a new mate only when the original dies. Courtship flights in late winter and early spring have the pair flying wide circles calling shrilly while the male dives steeply, climbs again and sometimes grasps her talons; the same nesting territory may be defended for years.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: The pair builds a stick nest of twigs lined with bark, pine needles, corn cobs, husks, stalks and catkins, 71 to 97 cm across and up to 90 cm tall, in a large tree 4 to 21 m up, on a cliff ledge 35 m or higher, or on a man-made structure. A clutch of one to five eggs is laid in spring about every second day, both parents incubate, and the female broods while the male brings most of the food.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Altricial nestlings emerge from the eggs over 2 to 4 days, leave the nest after 42 to 46 days, spend some 10 weeks learning to fly and hunt, and begin catching their own prey about 6 to 7 weeks after fledging.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: The birds tend to be territorial during winter and may shift range when food requires it, but they pass by one-by-one in migration rather than in groups.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: The species is a partial migrant: in most of Canada and Alaska they almost entirely vacate their breeding grounds, though birds in the Pacific Northwest, southern Alaska and Nova Scotia usually do not migrate, and spring northward movements may begin as early as late February.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Pairs construct a stick nest in a large tree 4-21 m up, or on a cliff ledge or man-made structure, 71-97 cm across; a clutch of one to five eggs is laid in spring.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Nestlings emerge 42-46 days after hatching; fledging, including learning to hunt, takes about 10 weeks.

vocalizations.description: A two- to three-second hoarse, rasping scream described as kree-eee-ar that begins at a high pitch and slurs downward, often compared to a steam whistle. Given while hunting or soaring, and loudest in annoyance or anger in response to a predator or a rival hawk intruding on its territory, and during courtship.
At close range a croaking, lower guh-runk instead of the full scream.
A wailing klee-uk food cry uttered by young hawks when the parents leave the nest.
A croaking guh-runk at close range; young hawks give a wailing klee-uk food cry when parents leave the nest.

taxonomy.note: Accipitridae, Buteo, (Gmelin, 1788). Described by Johann Friedrich Gmelin in 1788 as Falco jamaicensis from Latham's cream-coloured buzzard, based on a specimen from Jamaica; jamaicensis refers to that island. Buteo are medium-sized raptors with robust bodies and broad wings.

external.note: GBIF usage key 2480542 and iNaturalist taxon 5212; ITIS TSN 56263 from Wikidata P685.

conservation.note: 'One of the most common hawks in North America', with a population estimated at about one million in the United States, legally protected in Canada, Mexico and the United States by the Migratory Bird Treaty and with few natural predators as adults. This is consistent with Least Concern; no IUCN page was consulted because those are not openly licensed.

range.note: 'The red-tailed hawk breeds throughout most of the continent, from western Alaska and northern Canada to as far south as Panama and the West Indies.'

traits.limb_count.note: A bird: two legs are the limbs.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Soars and flies between perches, glides on broad wings, watches for prey from an elevated perch and swoops down to seize it, and walks on the ground only rarely. Hover is left out of locomotion_modes because the biped_winged body plan has no hover pose.

traits.nest_type.note: Platform: 'the pair constructs a stick nest in a high tree', 71 to 97 cm in diameter and up to 90 cm tall, built of twigs lined with bark, pine needles, corn cobs, husks, stalks and catkins, on a cliff ledge or a man-made structure as alternatives.

traits.perching.note: Its preferred habitat is mixed forest and field with high bluffs or trees used as perch sites, and it hunts by scanning from an elevated perch and swooping.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: about 940 g is under 1 kg, so Small.

traits.mass_kg.note: The mean of the two means the article reports for the largest compilation of measurements, males at 837 g and females at 1,040.7 g, giving about 939 g. The commonly quoted species-wide weights of 690 to 1,600 g are reported as about 15% too high.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Males may weigh from 690 to 1,300 g and females from 900 to 2,000 g; the record combines both.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Judgement, not a measurement. The article calls red-tailed hawks long-lived and notes that a falconer can keep one as a hunting companion for many years, but it gives no wild longevity figure and no openly licensed source was found, so 20 years is an authored estimate.

traits.diet.note: 'The red-tailed hawk preys on small mammals such as rodents and lagomorphs, but also opportunistically consumes birds, fish, reptiles, and amphibians', with rodents comprising up to 85% of the diet. Most common prey are mice, gophers, voles, chipmunks and squirrels; additional prey runs from lagomorphs, shrews and bats through pigeons, quail and corvids to reptiles, fish, crustaceans, insects and earthworms, which is where the invertebrate and fish shares come from. Carrion is not described for this species, so it is left out rather than guessed at.

traits.social.note: 'Pairs stay together for life, taking a new mate only when the original mate dies', and the same nesting territory may be defended by the pair for years; red-tailed hawks have also been observed to hunt in pairs, stalking opposite sides of a tree to flush a squirrel for the other.

traits.activity_pattern.note: A bird of prey that hunts by day from perches and while soaring; the great horned owl takes a similar niche nocturnally, but the differing nesting seasons and activity times mean there is usually no direct competition.

traits.defense.note: Authored. Adult hawks have few natural predators and the cry is loudest in response to a predator or a rival hawk intruding into its territory, so the species defends its perch, nest and airspace by vocal challenge and by driving off intruders rather than by fleeing.

traits.wariness.note: 'Unlike some other raptors, the red-tailed hawk is seemingly unfazed by considerable human activity and can nest and live in close proximity to large numbers of humans.'

habitat.use.note: Second only to the peregrine falcon in the use of diverse habitats in North America, occupying deserts, grasslands, coastal regions, mountains, foothills, coniferous and deciduous woodlands, agricultural fields and urban areas; it is absent from unbroken forest and the high Arctic, and spends its time on the wing and on high perches rather than on the ground.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Nests and roosts on high perches, bluffs and trees; preferred habitat is mixed forest and field with high bluffs or trees as perch sites.

habitat.resources.note: Predation weights from the diet paragraph; perch from the perch-site and perch-hunting description, and nest_platform from the large stick nest in a high tree. Weights are authored to match the diet shares.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Seemingly unfazed by human activity, nesting and living close to large numbers of people; found in cities where rock pigeons and brown rats support the population; highways with utility poles alongside treeless medians provided perfect perch-hunting habitat; and historic settlement patterns helped it by opening hunting areas while leaving woodlots for nest sites.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'The species is a partial migrant, as in most of their range in Canada and Alaska, they almost entirely vacate their breeding grounds', with coastal birds in the Pacific Northwest, southern Alaska and Nova Scotia usually resident, and birds territorial during winter.

seasonal.winter_fraction.note: 0.8 is an authored judgement: red-tailed hawks are resident year-round through much of the United States, including the Northeast, while birds breeding in Canada and Alaska largely leave, and the article gives no share for any one state.

seasonal.phases.note: Sexual maturity at two years; monogamy for life; courtship flights in late winter and early spring; a stick nest 4 to 21 m up in a large tree, on a cliff ledge 35 m or higher, or on a man-made structure, 71 to 97 cm across; a clutch of one to five eggs laid about every second day with both parents incubating; nestlings leaving after 42-46 days and about 10 weeks of learning to fly and hunt; and birds territorial in winter.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Altricial nestlings emerge from the eggs over 2 to 4 days and start to leave the nest after 42 to 46 days, so 70 days covers the nestling period to fledging; scale is an authored juvenile size.

vocalizations.scream.note: 'The cry of the red-tailed hawk is a two- to three-second, hoarse, rasping scream, described as kree-eee-ar, that begins at a high pitch and slurs downward... often described as sounding similar to a steam whistle.' It is given while hunting or soaring and loudest in annoyance or anger, including during courtship.

vocalizations.growl.note: 'At close range, it makes a croaking guh-runk.'

vocalizations.food_cry.note: 'Young hawks may utter a wailing klee-uk food cry when parents leave the nest.'

look.note: From the lead and the description: a stocky body with broad wings, and the eponymous tail 'uniformly brick-red above and light buff-orange below', which is the one feature that identifies the species. The model uses one dark brown adult plumage with a rufous tail and a darker belly band; the belly band is an authored device, since the article describes the plumage only briefly and one morph cannot show the fourteen subspecies. Proportions are authored.

behavior.note: A bespoke program ships with this record because none of the four shared programs fits a buteo. The perching-songbird program would have it forage by hopping on the ground and sing a territorial song, which a hawk never does; the ground-forager, anuran and seabird programs are worse still. fsm-perch-hunting-raptor-v1 gives it what the article describes: perching and scanning, dropping off the perch to seize prey, soaring, a hoarse scream at a threat or a rival, incubation and stick-nest building in spring and early summer, and roosting when the sun is well down. Distances and dwell times are authored.
